column2:
Your platform team maintains four internal agents: support triage, a sales assistant, an engineering copilot, and an ops bot. Each one hand-authors its own tool schemas and wrapper functions for the same ticket-tracker API, roughly 30 duplicated tool definitions per agent. A recent change to the tracker API forced coordinated fixes across all four codebases.

What is the primary architectural benefit of replacing these per-agent integrations with a single ticket-tracker MCP server?

A. Each agent's model will select tools more accurately, because MCP servers expose schemas in a format the model natively prefers.
B. The agents will no longer need an agentic loop, because the MCP server communicates with the model directly on their behalf.
C. Tool schemas and implementations are authored and maintained once inside the server, and every agent consumes them through an MCP client instead of duplicating integration code.
D. Each agent can call the tracker without tool-use messages, since MCP replaces tool use with direct model-to-API calls.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. MCP's core value is shifting the burden of defining and executing tools from each application to a dedicated server: the tracker integration is written and maintained in one place, and every agent discovers and calls the same pre-built tools through its client. Option A misstates what MCP changes; the schemas are ordinary tool schemas, and MCP does not by itself alter selection accuracy. Option B is wrong because each agent still runs its own conversation loop with the model; MCP only changes where tools live and run. Option D confuses the relationship: MCP is complementary to tool use, and the model still emits tool-use requests that are executed via the MCP client and server.

column2:
You configure Claude Desktop to connect to three MCP servers: an internal docs server, a ticket tracker, and a read-only database. A teammate reviewing your architecture diagram asks why it shows three MCP clients when there is only one application.

Which statement correctly describes the relationship?

A. The diagram is wrong; a host multiplexes every server through one shared client connection.
B. Claude Desktop is the host, and it instantiates one MCP client per server, each maintaining a dedicated connection to its corresponding server.
C. MCP clients execute tools locally, so an application needs one client per category of tool rather than one per server.
D. The extra clients exist for failover; a single client carries all of the traffic until its connection drops.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. In MCP's architecture the host is the AI application, and it creates one client for each server it connects to, with each client holding a dedicated one-to-one connection — three servers therefore means three clients. Option A describes a multiplexing model MCP does not use. Option C is doubly wrong: clients do not execute tools (servers do), and clients map to servers, not tool categories. Option D invents a redundancy scheme; multiple clients are the normal connection model, not standbys.

column2:
You are building an MCP server that exposes an engineer's on-laptop development database to Claude Code. The server will run on the same machine, launched by Claude Code as a subprocess at the start of each session.

Which transport is the standard fit for this deployment?

A. stdio, since the host launches the server as a local subprocess and the two exchange messages over standard input and output.
B. Streamable HTTP, since tool results and resource contents are too large to be returned reliably over a subprocess's pipes.
C. WebSockets, since a stdio connection permits only a single request and response before the subprocess must be relaunched.
D. A shared file that both processes poll for new messages, since MCP is transport agnostic and any local channel is acceptable.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. stdio is the transport designed for exactly this shape: a local server spawned by the host, communicating over standard input/output between processes on the same machine with no network in the path. Option B's premise is false; tool results flow over stdio routinely, and Streamable HTTP is the fit for remote servers serving many clients. Option C invents a limitation; stdio carries the full ongoing message exchange for the session. Option D misapplies transport agnosticism, which means the protocol works over multiple defined transports, not that ad hoc file polling is a supported mechanism.

column2:
Your team wrote its docs MCP server with the Python SDK. A sister team's agent is written in TypeScript, and it connects to your server and uses every tool without any changes on your side. An engineer asks how this works across languages.

What makes this interoperability possible?

A. The two SDKs share a common runtime layer that translates Python objects into TypeScript objects at the process boundary.
B. Claude recognizes MCP servers and adapts its tool-call format to whatever language each server is written in before emitting a call.
C. The client downloads the server's source code at connect time and regenerates typed bindings for its own language.
D. The MCP spec defines standard JSON-RPC message types, such as list-tools and call-tool, that any client or server can implement in any language.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. MCP's data layer is a JSON-RPC based exchange whose message types are defined by the specification; both sides speak that wire protocol, so implementation language is irrelevant. Option A invents a shared runtime; the SDKs are independent implementations of the same message contract. Option B places the adaptation in the model, but the model never talks to servers directly and the message format does not vary by language. Option C describes code generation that does not happen; the client learns about a server through protocol messages like the list-tools request, not by reading its source.

column2:
The team that owns your company's ticket-tracker MCP server ships four new tools overnight. The next morning your support agent, whose own code has not been redeployed, starts using all four tools in conversations.

Why are the new tools available without an agent release?

A. The agent's .mcp.json file caches every connected server's tool schemas and was regenerated automatically when the server changed.
B. The agent sends a list-tools request when it connects, so each session offers the model whatever the server currently exposes.
C. Anthropic refreshed the model's weights overnight, so the model itself now knows about the four new tool definitions.
D. The agent's build pipeline embeds server schemas at compile time, and a scheduled nightly rebuild picked up the new tool definitions.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Tool definitions are not baked into the client; the client asks the server what it offers each time it connects, so server-side additions appear in the very next session. Option A misunderstands the config file, which stores how to connect to servers, not their tool schemas. Option C attributes the change to the model, but models learn about available tools from the definitions sent with each request, not from retraining. Option D contradicts the stem — no redeploy occurred — and describes exactly the build-time embedding that MCP's runtime discovery replaces.

column2:
In a design review for a GitHub-connected assistant, a colleague objects: 'We can already give Claude tools that call the GitHub API directly — MCP just adds moving parts.' Covering repositories, pull requests, and issues would take your team roughly 25 hand-built tools.

What is the most accurate response?

A. MCP is required here, because a model cannot call an external API through tools your own team writes; only an MCP server can execute tool calls.
B. MCP produces measurably higher tool-selection accuracy, because servers expose schemas in a format the model has been trained to prefer.
C. Direct tool use is deprecated, and MCP is its designated replacement, so new integrations should not define tools by hand at all.
D. MCP is complementary to tool use: it moves authoring and maintaining those 25 tools into a dedicated server, often from the service provider, instead of your team.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. The honest case for MCP is about ownership and maintenance, not new model capability: the same tools exist either way, but with MCP they are written, executed, and updated inside a server your team merely connects to. Option A is false — hand-authored tools calling GitHub directly work fine, which is exactly the colleague's point. Option B claims an accuracy benefit MCP does not promise; selection quality depends on the definitions, not on who hosts them. Option C is wrong because tool use is not deprecated; MCP builds on it, and the model still makes ordinary tool calls.

column2:
Your ticket-tracker MCP server must support two consumers: individual engineers running Claude Code on their laptops, and a centrally hosted support agent that serves about 40 concurrent users from one deployment.

Which TWO transport and deployment decisions are correct? (Select TWO.)

A. For the laptops, ship a local server that each Claude Code instance launches itself and communicates with over stdio.
B. Point each laptop's stdio transport at the central host over the network, since stdio works across machines.
C. Run a Streamable HTTP server for the central deployment, since that transport is designed for remote servers serving many clients.
D. Avoid HTTP entirely, because the MCP spec defines stdio as the only supported transport.
column3:
Correct Answer: A and C. Options A and C pair each deployment with its intended transport: stdio is for local, same-machine processes where the host spawns the server, while Streamable HTTP is for remote servers that typically serve many clients at once. Option B is impossible as stated — stdio is standard input/output between processes on one machine, not a network protocol. Option D is factually wrong; the spec defines both stdio and Streamable HTTP transports, and a remote multi-user deployment is exactly where the HTTP transport belongs.

column2:
Your internal docs MCP server uses the Python SDK and defines 14 tools. The team also hand-maintains a separate JSON schema file per tool, and two production incidents last month traced to a schema advertising a parameter its function no longer accepts.

What is the most effective way to eliminate this class of drift?

A. Add a CI job that diffs each JSON schema file against its function signature and fails the build on any mismatch between the two.
B. Define each tool as an @mcp.tool-decorated function with typed parameters and Field descriptions, so the SDK generates the schema from the signature.
C. Drop the schemas and describe each tool's parameters in prose in the system prompt, so the model infers the input format from the description.
D. Keep both artifacts but have the model check its own arguments against the tool's docstring before every call and correct any mismatch.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. The Python SDK generates the JSON schema directly from the decorated function's type hints and Field descriptions, so the signature is the single source of truth and schema-versus-code drift cannot occur. Option A builds tooling to police a duplication the SDK makes unnecessary. Option C removes machine-enforced structure entirely, trading a solved problem for probabilistic parsing of prose. Option D relies on the model self-validating against documentation, exactly the kind of prompt-level compliance that drifting docs would quietly poison.

column2:
Your docs server exposes search_docs, which takes keywords and returns matching document IDs, and read_doc_contents, which returns one document by exact ID. Each has a one-line description: 'Searches documents' and 'Reads a document.' In test transcripts, the agent calls read_doc_contents with guessed, nonexistent IDs in about 20% of tasks instead of searching first.

What is the most effective first change?

A. Add a routing layer that classifies each user request and restricts which of the two tools the model may call.
B. Merge both into one find_or_read tool that falls back to keyword search whenever the given ID fails to resolve.
C. Rewrite both descriptions to state what input each expects — keywords versus an exact ID from a prior search — and when to use each.
D. Add eight few-shot example transcripts to the system prompt demonstrating correct search-then-read sequences.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Tool descriptions are the primary signal the model uses for tool selection, and these say nothing about where a valid ID comes from; stating that read_doc_contents requires an exact ID produced by search_docs fixes the root cause at the cheapest point. Option A is over-engineered before the zero-cost fix is tried and bypasses the model's own selection ability. Option B papers over the confusion by consolidating two clear operations into one blurrier tool. Option D adds standing token overhead to compensate for definitions that remain ambiguous, treating the symptom rather than the source.

column2:
Your support application does two things with customer data: it loads the customer's account summary into the first prompt of every single session, and it occasionally needs to search past tickets when the conversation calls for it.

How should these two needs map onto your MCP server design?

A. Expose ticket search as a tool the model invokes when it judges necessary, and expose the account summary as a resource that application code reads at session start.
B. Expose both as tools and add a system-prompt rule that the model must always call the account-summary tool before doing anything else in the session.
C. Expose both as resources, since account summaries and ticket search results are read-only customer data that application code can fetch on demand.
D. Expose ticket search as a tool and the account summary as a second tool, letting the model decide each session whether the summary is worth loading.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. The dividing line is who decides when the operation runs: ticket search depends on conversational judgment, so it belongs to the model as a tool, while the summary load happens every session unconditionally, so application code should perform it deterministically rather than hoping the model does. Option B enforces a deterministic requirement through prompt instructions, which is probabilistic where a guarantee is available. Option C breaks the search case — only the model knows mid-conversation when searching is warranted, and app code cannot anticipate it. Option D delegates a step that must happen 100% of the time to a probabilistic chooser.

column2:
A ticket-tracker MCP server exposes get_data, get_data_v2, and fetch_info. Logs show the model splitting equivalent requests across all three, and 15% of calls still go to the deprecated get_data.

What is the most effective fix?

A. Keep the names and add a system-prompt note explaining what each of the three variants actually does and when the model should prefer it.
B. Add a keyword-based pre-parser that maps user phrasing to the correct tool before the model sees the request.
C. Delete get_data_v2 and fetch_info so that only a single tool remains regardless of what each one does.
D. Rename the tools to distinct, purpose-revealing names such as search_tickets and get_ticket_details, with descriptions stating when each applies.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Names and descriptions are the interface the model selects against; three near-synonymous labels give it nothing to discriminate on, so renaming to distinct, intent-revealing names with matching descriptions removes the ambiguity at its source. Option A leaves the confusing surface intact and patches it with standing prompt text, a weaker and costlier signal. Option B is an over-engineered bypass of the model's language understanding for a problem caused by bad labels. Option C consolidates blindly — if the tools do different jobs, collapsing them discards capability instead of clarifying it.

column2:
You are defining process_refund for a customer-support resolution agent. Refund mistakes are costly, and the tool will sit alongside get_customer and lookup_order on the same MCP server.

Which TWO elements of the tool definition contribute most to reliable use by the model? (Select TWO.)

A. A single free-form request string parameter that the server parses, so the model is never blocked by schema validation.
B. Typed, constrained parameters — order ID, amount, reason — declared in the input schema with a description for each.
C. A tool description stating what the tool does, its prerequisites such as a verified customer and located order, and how it differs from the neighboring lookup tools.
D. A deliberately minimal one-line description, keeping the overall tool list short enough for the model to read completely.
column3:
Correct Answer: B and C. Option B makes the expected input machine-checkable and tells the model exactly what to supply, and Option C is the steering surface that governs when the model reaches for this tool rather than its neighbors — together they cover the two failure modes that matter most for a high-stakes action: malformed calls and misselection. Option A abandons schema validation, inviting ambiguous inputs into precisely the tool where mistakes are most expensive. Option D repeats a documented anti-pattern: minimal descriptions are a primary cause of tool misuse, and the tokens saved are trivial next to the reliability lost.

column2:
A teammate proposes collapsing your document server's read_doc_contents and edit_document tools into one document_op tool with an action parameter set to 'read' or 'edit', plus optional old_string and new_string fields, arguing that fewer tools are always easier for the model.

What is the strongest reason to keep the two separate tools?

A. The MCP specification caps the size of a tool's input schema, and a combined tool carrying both read and edit parameters would exceed that limit.
B. Each operation keeps its own precise schema and description, so a read cannot carry edit-only parameters and the model gets a clear signal for when each applies.
C. A combined tool could not validate its inputs or raise an execution error for a missing document, since validation only works on single-purpose schemas.
D. Keeping two tools halves the token cost of tool definitions in every request, because each definition is sent only when its operation is relevant.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. One tool per distinct operation keeps the contract crisp: the edit schema can require old_string and new_string, the read schema cannot accept them, and each description covers exactly one behavior — stronger validation and a clearer selection signal than a mode flag with optional fields. Option A invents a limit; the specification sets no cap on input schema size, and a merged schema would be modest anyway. Option C is false; a merged tool could still validate its inputs and return execution errors, just with murkier conditional rules. Option D gets the mechanics backwards — every tool definition is sent with every request, so two definitions are not cheaper, and the real benefit is clarity, not size.

column2:
Your edit_document tool performs exact find-and-replace with doc_id, old_string, and new_string parameters. In production, roughly 30% of edits silently change nothing because the model supplies old_string values with paraphrased wording or normalized whitespace that never match the document.

What is the most effective first fix?

A. Give old_string a Field description stating that the text must match the document exactly, including whitespace, copied verbatim from a prior read.
B. Wrap the edit in a server-side loop that retries up to five times with the same arguments whenever the replacement changes nothing.
C. Upgrade to a larger model, since the paraphrasing comes from model capability and stronger models reproduce source text verbatim.
D. Make the server fuzzy-match old_string and silently apply the replacement at the closest location it finds, so edits never no-op.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Parameter-level descriptions steer how the model constructs arguments; the model paraphrases because nothing tells it exact matching is required, so documenting the exact-match contract — including whitespace — on the parameter fixes the failure where it originates. Option B re-submits the same doomed arguments; retrying without new information cannot change the outcome. Option C reaches for a bigger model to compensate for an unstated requirement no model can reliably infer. Option D trades silent no-ops for something worse: silent approximate edits that can alter text the user never intended.

column2:
Your MCP server's lookup_order tool receives an order number in the wrong format from the model. You are deciding how the server should report the failure so the agent can recover.

Which reporting mechanism is correct for this case?

A. A JSON-RPC protocol error, because a badly formatted order number makes the whole request malformed, and the transport layer should reject it.
B. A normal result containing an empty order object, so the conversation continues without alarming the model or triggering a retry.
C. A tool result flagged isError: true whose text explains the expected order-number format, so the model can correct its arguments and retry.
D. Closing the connection so the client re-initializes with a clean session, since a malformed argument indicates the session state is corrupted.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. The spec distinguishes protocol errors — structural problems like unknown tools or malformed requests — from tool execution errors such as input validation failures, which are returned inside the result with isError: true and actionable text precisely so the model can self-correct. A wrong order-number value inside a well-formed call is an execution error, and Option C handles it that way. Option A misclassifies it: the JSON-RPC request itself is valid, and protocol errors are the category models are least able to fix. Option B silently fabricates an empty success, hiding the failure the model needs to see. Option D destroys session state over a routine, recoverable validation problem.

column2:
Telemetry on your support agent shows process_refund failing in 18% of attempts. Every failure returns the same text: 'Error: operation failed.' In transcripts the model responds by retrying the identical call, then apologizing to the customer without resolving anything.

What change most improves the agent's recovery rate?

A. Suppress the error and return a neutral 'request received' acknowledgment, so conversations stay positive and the model stops retrying.
B. Cap tool retries at one in the client and route every failed refund directly to a human review queue with the transcript attached.
C. Ask the model to rate its own confidence after each failure and retry only when confidence exceeds 0.8, escalating to a human otherwise.
D. Return error text naming the failed check, the offending value, and a valid next step, such as 'exceeds the $500 limit for unverified accounts; verify the customer first.'
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Tool execution errors are supposed to carry actionable feedback the model can use to adjust and retry; a generic status gives it nothing, which is why it repeats the same call. Option D supplies the missing information — which rule failed, by how much, and what to do next — enabling genuine self-correction. Option A is silent suppression: the model will tell the customer the refund succeeded. Option B escalates every failure, including the large fraction the model could fix itself once informed, and still leaves the error text useless. Option C leans on self-reported confidence, which is not a reliable routing signal and adds no new facts about the failure.

column2:
Your ticket-tracker tool has two failure modes: upstream timeouts, about 60% of errors and usually resolving within seconds, and invalid ticket IDs, the remaining 40%. Both currently return 'Error: request failed.' The agent retries invalid IDs pointlessly and abandons timed-out requests that a retry would have completed.

How should the server's error results change?

A. Distinguish the cases in the error text: label timeouts as transient and worth retrying, and label invalid IDs as validation errors that need a real ID from the search tool.
B. Return isError: false for the timeouts, so the model does not treat a temporary upstream condition as a failure of its own request.
C. Mark every error as retryable and have the client retry all failures three times with exponential backoff before surfacing anything to the model.
D. Return an empty ticket object for both cases, so the conversation always continues and the model can decide on its own whether to retry.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. The two failure classes demand opposite recoveries — retry the transient one, change strategy on the validation one — so the error result must say which class occurred and what to do about it; that is what makes an error actionable. Option B mislabels a failure as success, leaving the model to treat missing data as a completed lookup. Option C burns retries on invalid IDs that can never succeed and still gives the model no guidance afterward. Option D silently suppresses both errors and hands the model fabricated empty data, the least recoverable outcome of all.

column2:
You built a custom MCP client for an internal agent. When a tool result arrives flagged isError: true, the client swallows it and sends Claude the text 'tool temporarily unavailable' no matter what the actual message said. Evals show the agent re-attempting the same malformed call for three consecutive turns.

What should the client do instead?

A. Convert every isError result into a JSON-RPC protocol error so the failure is handled at the transport layer.
B. Pass the execution error's actual content through to the model as the tool result, so it can adjust its arguments or change approach.
C. Drop errored calls from the conversation history entirely to keep the model's context clean.
D. Terminate the session after the first errored call and restart the conversation again from scratch.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Clients should surface tool execution errors to the model because that feedback is what enables self-correction; this client replaces a presumably specific message with a misleading generic one, so the model keeps repeating a call it believes merely hit a temporary outage. Option A moves the failure into the protocol-error category, the kind models are least equipped to act on, and hides it from the conversation. Option C removes even the evidence that something failed, guaranteeing repetition. Option D throws away the whole session over a routine recoverable failure rather than letting the model retry with better arguments.

• Build an MCP client

column2:
Your docs MCP server must support a client UI that lists all document IDs in an autocomplete menu and fetches one document's contents when the user mentions it. There are about 200 documents averaging 4 KB each.

How should the server expose this data?

A. One direct resource that returns every document's full contents, so the client always has everything it might need.
B. One templated resource docs://documents/{doc_id}; the client can iterate over possible IDs to assemble its menu.
C. Two tools, list_docs and read_doc, which the model calls whenever the UI needs fresh data to display.
D. Two resources: a direct resource returning the list of document IDs, and a templated resource keyed by doc_id returning a single document's contents.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. The working pattern is one resource per distinct read operation: a static listing gets a direct (fixed-URI) resource, and fetch-one-by-ID gets a templated resource whose URI parameter selects the document. Option A ships roughly 800 KB of content to draw a menu that needs only names. Option B has no listing operation at all — the client cannot know which IDs exist to iterate, and hundreds of reads to build a menu is wasteful. Option C routes app-controlled UI data through model tool calls, adding latency and a probabilistic dependency to something application code should fetch deterministically.

References:
• MCP spec: resources
• Build an MCP server
• MCP server concepts

column2:
In the Python SDK you define a templated resource with @mcp.resource('docs://documents/{doc_id}'), but the decorated function's signature is def fetch_doc(document_id: str). The server raises an error at startup while registering this resource.

What is wrong?

A. The placeholder name must match the parameter name: the SDK parses the {doc_id} value out of the requested URI and passes it as the doc_id keyword argument.
B. Templated resources cannot accept string parameters, so the ID segment must be declared as an integer and converted inside the function.
C. The function must accept the full requested URI as its only argument and parse the document ID out of it itself, as the SDK passes URIs whole.
D. Templated resources additionally require each URI parameter to be declared in a separate JSON schema passed to the decorator.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. With templated resources the SDK does the URI parsing for you: each name inside braces must correspond to a function parameter of exactly that name, because the value parsed from the requested URI is passed as that keyword argument. The SDK checks this correspondence when the decorator registers the template and raises on a mismatch, so {doc_id} needs a doc_id parameter, not document_id. Option B invents a type restriction; string parameters are the normal case. Option C describes the manual parsing the SDK exists to eliminate. Option D contradicts how the SDK works — the decorator and the function signature are the entire definition, with no separately maintained schema.

References:

column2:
In your CLI chat app, typing the @ character must instantly display the current list of documents in an autocomplete menu, before any message is sent to Claude.

Which MCP primitive should back this feature, and why?

A. A tool, so the model can fetch the document list whenever it judges that the UI is likely to need it.
B. A prompt that returns the document list to the client inside a pre-written assistant message that the client renders as the menu.
C. A resource, because this is app-controlled data: application code decides when to fetch it and renders the menu with no model in the loop.
D. A system-prompt preamble listing every document, refreshed whenever the server process restarts.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Autocomplete at keystroke time is a pure application concern — the app knows the moment it needs the data and simply reads it — which is exactly the app-controlled role resources fill; populating a document picker is the course's canonical resource example. Option A cannot work: no model is running when the user types @, and tools put timing under the model's control. Option B misuses prompts, which are user-invoked message templates for workflows, not a data feed. Option D goes stale between restarts and pays for the full listing in every request whether or not the menu is opened.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.4

References:
• MCP server concepts
• MCP spec: resources

column2:
Transcript analysis of your docs chatbot shows that in 70% of conversations the user names the exact document they want, as in 'summarize @report.pdf.' The agent still makes two tool round trips per request — one to list documents, one to read the named one — adding about four seconds of latency.

Which change best removes this overhead for those conversations?

A. Instruct the model in the system prompt to skip the listing call and read the named document directly whenever the user has already named one.
B. When the user mentions a document, have the application read its templated resource and place the contents directly in the prompt sent to Claude.
C. Move to a model with a larger context window, so that each tool round trip carries less overhead and completes faster.
D. Cache the full contents of every document in the system prompt when the session starts, so the model never needs to list or read anything.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. When the user has already identified the document, fetching it is deterministic — application code can read the resource and inject the contents into the prompt, eliminating both exploratory tool calls; this is precisely the mention pattern the course builds with resources. Option A is prompt-level guidance that still leaves at least one model-driven round trip and no guarantee. Option C confuses context capacity with round-trip latency; window size does not make tool cycles faster. Option D front-loads every document into every request, exploding token cost and going stale as documents change.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.4

References:
• MCP spec: resources
• MCP server concepts

column2:
Your direct resource docs://documents returns a Python list of IDs; the SDK serializes the return value, and the server declares MIME type application/json. In your client, the autocomplete menu renders a single entry containing the literal text ['report.pdf', 'plan.md', ...] instead of one entry per document.

What is the root cause?

A. The client ignores the declared MIME type: for application/json it should deserialize the returned text with json.loads before rendering.
B. The server should return the raw list object instead of letting the SDK serialize it, since resource contents are transmitted as native objects.
C. Lists require a templated resource that the client reads once per item; a direct resource can only ever return a single item.
D. The model should be asked to parse the returned string into menu options, since interpreting resource contents is the model's job.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Resource contents arrive as text, and the MIME type is the server's hint about how to interpret that text; a client that sees application/json must parse the JSON string into a data structure, which this client is skipping. Option B fights the protocol — return values are serialized to strings for transport by design, so returning a raw object is not an option on the wire. Option C confuses resource addressing (fixed versus parameterized URI) with payload shape; a direct resource can happily return a serialized list. Option D drags the model into an app-controlled rendering path where it has no role.

column2:
A teammate's pull request adds a templated resource docs://documents/{doc_id}/archive whose handler moves the document into an archive store and returns a confirmation string, so that 'the app can archive things with a single resource read.'

What is the main design problem?

A. The URI has too many path segments; a resource template may carry only one placeholder, and it must be the final segment.
B. Archiving must be exposed as a prompt instead, because a person ultimately initiates the action and prompts are the user-controlled primitive.
C. Resources exist to expose data for reading; an operation with side effects like archiving belongs in a tool, as an explicit, schema-described action.
D. The handler returns a plain string, but resource handlers are required to return JSON so clients can deserialize them by MIME type.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Resources are the read primitive — clients ask for data at a URI and expect the fetch to be safe — so hiding a mutation behind a read breaks the contract every client assumes; state-changing operations are what tools are for. Option A invents template restrictions; placeholders may appear in any segment and a template is not limited to one. Option B confuses surfacing with execution — a user-initiated flow may be started via a prompt, but the archive operation itself would still run as a tool, not as the prompt. Option D is false; MIME types exist precisely because resources legitimately return plain text, JSON, or other formats.

column2:
Your ticket application needs two behaviors: rendering the current ticket queue in a sidebar whenever the app refreshes it, and letting Claude change a ticket's status mid-conversation once a customer's issue is resolved.

Which TWO primitive choices are correct? (Select TWO.)

A. Expose the queue as a resource that application code reads each time it refreshes the sidebar.
B. Expose the queue as a tool so the model can fetch it whenever it believes the sidebar has gone stale.
C. Expose status changes as a prompt that returns the updated ticket inside a pre-written assistant message.
D. Expose status changes as a tool that the model invokes with a ticket ID and the new status value.
column3:
Correct Answer: A and D. Option A matches the queue to the app-controlled primitive: the application knows when it refreshes the sidebar and simply reads the data, with no model involved. Option D matches the status change to the model-controlled primitive: deciding mid-conversation that a ticket is resolved is exactly the judgment tools delegate to Claude. Option B hands UI freshness to the model, which is not even running when the app repaints and has no visibility into the sidebar. Option C misuses prompts, which are user-invoked message templates — they deliver instructions to the model and cannot themselves execute a state change.

column2:
Support leads want a 'draft escalation email' action in your chat client: an operator explicitly triggers it from a menu, and Claude then walks through gathering the case details and writing the email in the team's standard format.

Which MCP primitive fits this feature?

A. A tool, so the model can start the escalation workflow on its own whenever it detects rising frustration in the conversation.
B. A prompt, the user-controlled primitive: the client surfaces it as a command or button, and it returns a tested message sequence that drives the workflow.
C. A resource containing the email template, which the application fetches and displays when the session starts so the operator can fill it in.
D. A dedicated escalation agent that monitors every conversation and takes over whenever escalation seems warranted, so operators never trigger it.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. The defining requirement is that a person initiates the workflow, and user-controlled invocation is precisely what prompts are for: the client exposes them as buttons or slash commands, and invoking one returns curated messages that drive the multi-step task. Option A moves the trigger to the model and uses inferred sentiment as the signal, when the requirement is an explicit operator action. Option C supplies static data but no invocable workflow. Option D is heavy over-engineering — a monitoring agent — for what a predefined, user-triggered prompt already does.

column2:
Users of your document chatbot can already type 'convert report.pdf to Markdown' and get an acceptable result. A teammate therefore argues that the proposed /format server prompt adds nothing.

What is the strongest counterargument?

A. Without a server-defined prompt, Claude cannot reliably chain the read and edit tools, because tool sequencing is only guaranteed inside prompts.
B. Server prompts run the conversion on the server itself, so the workflow completes without spending model tokens or a conversation turn.
C. The server team can ship a tested, evaluated prompt tuned to its domain, so results are consistently strong instead of depending on how each user words the request.
D. Slash commands are the only mechanism through which a client is permitted to pass arguments such as a document name to a server.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. The point of MCP prompts is to package the server author's prompt-engineering expertise: a tuned, evaluated instruction outperforms the average user's ad hoc phrasing, and shipping it with the server raises the floor for everyone. Option A is false — free-text requests already trigger the same tools, as the stem itself demonstrates. Option B misunderstands the mechanism; a prompt returns messages and Claude still performs the work, tools included. Option D invents a protocol restriction; slash commands are just one client surface, and argument passing is not limited to them.

column2:
Your /format slash command works, but every invocation reformats report.pdf regardless of which document the user selects, because the document name is written directly into the prompt template string on the server.

What is the correct mechanism for making the prompt document-specific?

A. Have the client string-replace report.pdf with the selected document name in the returned messages before forwarding them to Claude.
B. Define one prompt per document, such as format_report and format_plan, so each carries its own template and the user picks the matching command.
C. Send the prompt as is and let Claude ask the user which document they meant in a follow-up turn before it calls the read tool.
D. Declare a doc_id argument on the prompt; the client sends the selected value with its get-prompt request and the server interpolates it.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Prompts are parameterized templates: the client sends argument values with the get-prompt request, the server interpolates them into the template, and the returned messages arrive ready to send — that round trip is the designed mechanism for dynamic content. Option A makes every client reverse-engineer the template's internals, breaking the encapsulation that lets any client use the server's prompts. Option B multiplies prompts per document and goes stale the moment documents are added. Option C spends an extra model turn recovering information the user already provided at invocation time.

column2:
You shipped generate_weekly_report as a tool on your analytics MCP server. Logs show Claude occasionally invoking it mid-conversation when users merely mention the word 'report,' and stakeholders want the workflow to run only when a person explicitly asks for it.

What is the best architectural change?

A. Re-expose the workflow as an MCP prompt surfaced as a slash command, so a deliberate user action starts it and its messages steer Claude through the steps.
B. Keep the tool and add a system-prompt rule stating that it must only be called when the user explicitly requests a report.
C. Keep the tool but require the model to state its confidence that a report is wanted, invoking only above 90%.
D. Move the workflow into a resource that the application fetches automatically every Monday morning and injects into the conversation.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. The problem is invocation authority: a tool is model-controlled by definition, so as long as the workflow is a tool the model may fire it on a hunch; re-modeling it as a prompt makes invocation user-controlled, which is exactly the stakeholder requirement. Option B leaves the authority with the model and papers over it with prompt instructions that will probabilistically fail. Option C gates the decision on self-reported confidence, an unreliable signal that still leaves the model in charge. Option D changes the trigger to a schedule nobody asked for, and resources expose data rather than multi-step workflows.

column2:
While testing /format, a developer inspects the get-prompt response expecting to find the reformatted document. Instead it contains a single user message instructing Claude to fetch the document with the read tool, rewrite it in Markdown, and save it with the edit tool. They file a bug titled 'prompt did not do anything.'

What should you explain?

A. The server is misconfigured; a correctly configured server executes the prompt's instructions itself and returns the finished document.
B. The prompt is missing a MIME type declaration, so the client cannot decode the finished Markdown document that the response carries.
C. This is correct behavior: a prompt returns messages for the client to send to Claude, and the work then happens in the conversation through tool calls.
D. The prompt should be converted into a templated resource, since only resources are able to return document contents to the client.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Prompts are pre-written conversation inputs, not remote procedures: get-prompt hands back messages, the client forwards them to Claude, and Claude then does the actual reading, rewriting, and saving via tools. Option A inverts the contract — no execution happens inside get-prompt on any correctly built server. Option B borrows MIME types from resources; they describe resource payloads, not prompt messages. Option D swaps in the read primitive when the feature is a workflow: a resource could serve the raw document but could never orchestrate reformatting and saving it.

column2:
Your client renders its slash-command autocomplete from a hardcoded array containing only 'format'. The server team ships new summarize and translate prompts; users of your client never see them, while another team's client offers all three immediately.

What change brings your client in line with intended MCP behavior?

A. Subscribe to the server team's release notes and update the hardcoded command array each sprint, shipping a client release for each new prompt.
B. Call the list-prompts operation when the session connects and build the command menu from the result, re-listing on each new session.
C. Ask the model at session start to guess which prompts the server most likely provides, and render its answer as the command menu.
D. Read the server's source files from disk at startup and parse the decorator names into a command list, so the menu tracks the code.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Prompts are discoverable the same way tools are: the client asks the server what it offers via list-prompts and renders its UI from the live answer, which is why the other client picked up all three commands with zero changes. Option A institutionalizes manual synchronization and guarantees lag. Option C invites hallucinated commands; the model has no knowledge of a server's prompt catalog. Option D breaks the protocol boundary entirely and is impossible for any server that is not running from local source.

column2:
You are adding three tools to a new docs MCP server. Your only test path today is launching the full CLI chatbot, chatting until Claude happens to call each tool, and reading logs — roughly ten minutes per iteration, with API costs on every run.

What is the standard faster loop?

A. After each edit, run scripted evals that send the tool schemas and sample prompts to the Claude API and grade whether the right tool was called.
B. Add verbose print statements to every tool and keep exercising them through chatbot conversations, reading the logs after each run.
C. Point a second chatbot instance at the server so that two models exercise the tools in parallel and halve the wait per iteration.
D. Run mcp dev on the server file and use the MCP Inspector in the browser to list the tools and invoke each one with chosen parameters.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. The Inspector exists for exactly this: an in-browser debugger, launched with mcp dev, that connects to your server so you can invoke tools directly with hand-picked inputs and see results immediately, before any client integration. Option A keeps the model in the loop for what is currently a server-correctness question, slower and costlier than direct invocation. Option B adds visibility but leaves the ten-minute, conversation-driven cycle intact. Option C doubles the expensive path instead of replacing it.

column2:
Before integrating a teammate's ticket-tracker MCP server, you get one hour with the MCP Inspector. The team lists four risks it wants checked during that hour.

Which risk can the Inspector directly validate?

A. That each tool executes correctly when invoked with valid parameters and returns the expected output.
B. That Claude will select search_tickets rather than get_ticket_details when users ask keyword questions.
C. That the server sustains 50 concurrent client connections without latency regressions under load.
D. That the production client's session cleanup logic closes its connections properly on shutdown.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. The Inspector connects you directly to the server and lets you manually invoke its tools, resources, and prompts with chosen inputs and observe the results — so per-tool execution correctness is squarely within its scope. Option B is a model-behavior question; the Inspector never involves Claude, so tool selection can only be tested with the model in the loop. Option C is a load-testing concern beyond a manual, single-user debugger. Option D lives in the client codebase, which the Inspector replaces rather than exercises.

column2:
In the Inspector you connect to your docs server and open the Resources section. Listing resources shows only docs://documents; your new templated resource docs://documents/{doc_id} is absent, and you begin suspecting the decorator is broken.

What is the most likely explanation?

A. Templated resources only appear in the listing after a real client has read them at least once, because the Inspector caches known URIs.
B. The Inspector lists direct resources and resource templates separately; the templated resource is under the templates listing, where you supply a doc_id.
C. Templated resources cannot be exercised in the Inspector at all, because their parameters can only be supplied by a model at run time.
D. A resource must declare an application/json MIME type before the Inspector will display it, and this template declares none.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Static resources and resource templates are enumerated separately: listing resources returns the fixed-URI ones, while templates appear in their own listing, where the Inspector accepts the parameter value before performing the read. Option A invents a usage precondition that does not exist. Option C is backwards — the Inspector's parameter fields exist precisely so a human can supply values like doc_id by hand. Option D confuses the MIME type, a deserialization hint about the payload, with visibility in listings.

column2:
Your edit_document tool returns only a success message, never the document text. You are investigating a report that some edits do not stick, and you want to confirm in the Inspector whether a specific find-and-replace actually changed the stored document.

What is the right verification flow?

A. Run edit_document and trust its success message, since the Inspector verifies a tool's side effects automatically after each call.
B. Run the edit through the production chatbot instead and ask Claude to confirm whether its own edit worked as intended.
C. In the Inspector, run edit_document with the target parameters, then invoke read_doc_contents on the same document and check for the change.
D. Restart the server after each edit to flush pending writes, then look for the change in the server's startup logs.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Because the edit tool's return value only signals that it ran, verifying the side effect means reading the state back: invoke the edit, then the read tool on the same document, and compare — the same two-step check the course demonstrates in the Inspector. Option A trusts a success message to prove a content change it does not contain; the Inspector performs no automatic side-effect verification. Option B substitutes the model's self-report for direct observation. Option D adds a restart ritual that verifies nothing — logs do not show document contents, and restarting can even discard in-memory state.

column2:
Your hand-rolled MCP client spawns the server subprocess and immediately writes a list-tools request to its stdin. The request intermittently hangs or errors, while the SDK's ClientSession-based reference client works against the same server every time.

What step is your client missing?

A. A fixed two-second startup delay before the first request, giving the subprocess enough time to load its tools before it reads stdin.
B. Retrying the list-tools request with exponential backoff until the server begins answering, since stdio servers accept requests only once warm.
C. Writing each request twice, since stdio transports drop the first message written after a process launch while the pipe is still buffering.
D. The initialization handshake: an initialize request and response exchanging protocol version and capabilities, then an initialized notification.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. MCP connections begin with a required initialization phase: the client sends an initialize request carrying its protocol version and capabilities, receives the server's capabilities in response, and confirms with an initialized notification; only then do operational requests like list-tools proceed, and the SDK's session performs this handshake for you on connect. Options A and B treat a protocol precondition as a timing flake — delays and retries may mask symptoms, but the connection is still unestablished by the rules. Option C invents a lossy-first-message behavior that stdio does not have.

column2:
Your client assumes every MCP server implements tools, resources, and prompts. Connected to a minimal tools-only server, it calls list-prompts at startup and treats the resulting failure as fatal — aborting the session even though every tool works.

What is the correct fix?

A. Read the capabilities the server declared during initialization and only exercise the features it actually advertised.
B. Require server teams to implement all three primitives before your client will accept a connection to them.
C. Wrap list-prompts in a retry loop, since prompt support may finish loading shortly after server startup.
D. Delegate the check to the model by asking Claude at session start whether this server provides prompts.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Initialization is a capability negotiation: the server's initialize response tells the client which optional features — tools, resources, prompts — this particular server supports, and a well-behaved client consults that declaration instead of assuming the full set. Option B inverts the fix by demanding servers change to satisfy a faulty client assumption; the primitives are optional by design. Option C misreads a permanent capability absence as a transient warm-up condition. Option D asks the model to know something it cannot observe; capability information arrives through the protocol, not the conversation.

column2:
Your CLI chatbot connects to the docs MCP server successfully, but Claude answers every document question from general knowledge and never calls the read tool. Request logs show each call to Claude contains only the system prompt and the user's message.

What is the first thing to fix in the loop?

A. Add a line to the system prompt telling Claude that a document server is connected and that it should call the read tool for document questions.
B. Fetch the server's tool definitions through the client's list-tools function and pass them in the tools parameter of each request to Claude.
C. Reduce the sampling temperature so that the model stops improvising answers from general knowledge and prefers the connected tools.
D. Configure the MCP server to push tool invocations to Claude directly whenever the documents change, bypassing the client loop.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. A model can only use tools that are passed to it in the request; the loop must first gather the server's tools via the client and send them alongside the query, which is precisely the step this codebase skipped. Option A tells the model tools exist without giving it any to call — there is still nothing in the request to select. Option C tunes decoding for what is a missing-input problem. Option D reverses the architecture: servers respond to client requests and never talk to the model.

column2:
In your agent loop, Claude responds with a tool-use request for read_doc_contents, and your client executes it through call-tool and receives the document text. But the chat then stalls: the transcript ends at Claude's tool-use turn, and in 100% of tool-using conversations the user sees no answer.

What is missing from the loop?

A. A larger max-tokens setting, so the final answer can fit into the same response as the tool call instead of being cut off.
B. A parser that extracts Claude's final answer text from within the tool-use message itself, where it is embedded alongside the call.
C. Sending the tool's output back to Claude as a tool result in a follow-up message, and continuing the loop until a final text response.
D. A system-prompt instruction telling Claude to answer the question and call the tool within a single turn, so no follow-up is needed.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. A tool-use response is the midpoint of the cycle, not the end: the client must execute the call, return the result to the model in the next message, and let the model produce its final answer — this loop executes the tool but never completes the round trip. Option A misdiagnoses; no answer was truncated because none has been generated yet. Option B tries to parse an answer out of a message that by definition contains a request, not a conclusion. Option D asks the model to answer before it has the document, which is the situation tools exist to prevent.

column2:
A nightly batch job opens a fresh connection to your stdio MCP server for each of 500 documents, using the SDK's ClientSession directly. Over the run it leaves more and more orphaned server subprocesses behind, and the job increasingly hangs at exit.

Which practice addresses this?

A. Wrap the session in a client class whose async context-manager enter and exit own connect and cleanup, so each session is released when its work finishes.
B. Let the operating system reap the orphaned subprocesses when the job's main process finally exits, since stdio servers hold no other resources.
C. Remove the explicit cleanup code entirely, since a ClientSession closes its transport and subprocess automatically once it is garbage collected.
D. Add a scheduled task on the machine that kills any stray server processes once every hour, so the job never accumulates more than an hour's worth.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. A ClientSession represents a live connection that requires explicit teardown, and the standard practice is to wrap it in a class owning connect and cleanup via async enter and exit — the course's client class exists for exactly this reason, guaranteeing deterministic release per session. Option B waits on an exit that the leaked resources are themselves preventing. Option C bets on garbage collection to perform cleanup the SDK requires you to do. Option D is out-of-band process slaughter that treats the symptom while the job keeps leaking.

column2:
A code review of your team's custom agent finds two problems: the tool schemas sent to Claude were copied into the codebase by hand months ago and no longer match the server, causing schema-mismatch failures in 9% of calls; and when Claude requests a tool, the agent runs its own local reimplementation of the tool's logic, which has drifted from the server's behavior.

Which TWO changes fix the architecture? (Select TWO.)

A. Paste the server's current schemas into the system prompt and diff them by hand against the server at each release, so drift is caught before deploy.
B. Fetch tool definitions from the server at session start through the client's list-tools call, so Claude always sees exactly what the server currently exposes.
C. Cap the loop at one tool call per conversation to limit the blast radius of any remaining drift, and log every mismatch for manual review.
D. Route every tool-use request from Claude through the client's call-tool function, so the server executes its own tools and returns the results.
column3:
Correct Answer: B and D. Options B and D restore the two halves of MCP's contract: definitions are discovered live from the server rather than vendored, which ends schema drift, and execution happens on the server that owns the tools, which ends logic drift. Option A remains manual and stale, and the system prompt is not where tool definitions belong — they are structured request inputs, not prose. Option C is an iteration cap masquerading as safety; it truncates legitimate multi-step work while both kinds of drift continue on the one call it still allows.

column2:
Your team of eight shares one repository, and you want your internal docs MCP server available automatically in Claude Code for every engineer who clones it, with no per-machine setup steps.

How should the server be configured?

A. Each engineer adds the server at user scope, so that it follows them across all of their projects, including this repository.
B. Each engineer adds the server at local scope during onboarding, with the exact claude mcp add command documented in the README.
C. Add it at project scope, which writes it to a .mcp.json file at the repository root that is checked into version control.
D. Paste the server's launch command into the repository's CLAUDE.md, which is committed, so Claude Code starts the server when it is needed.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Project scope exists for exactly this: the configuration lives in .mcp.json at the repository root, is committed like any other file, and every teammate who pulls the repo gets the server without manual steps. Option A is per-person setup that also spreads a project-specific server into unrelated projects. Option B still requires all eight engineers to perform documented manual setup, which is what you are trying to eliminate. Option D puts a shell command into model instructions — CLAUDE.md guides Claude's behavior and does not register MCP servers with the client.

A security review flags your repository: the committed .mcp.json entry for the ticket-tracker server contains a real API token in its env block. The team still wants the shared, checked-in configuration to keep working for everyone.

What is the correct remediation?

A. Reference the token as ${TRACKER_API_TOKEN} in .mcp.json, so the committed file expands a variable that each engineer sets locally.
B. Keep the token committed but restrict repository access to current team members, rotating the token whenever someone leaves.
C. Move the server entry to user scope on each laptop and share the token through the team chat during setup, keeping .mcp.json token-free.
D. Delete the env block and hardcode the token inside the server's own source code, which the security review did not scan.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. .mcp.json supports environment-variable expansion precisely so shared configuration can be committed without embedding secrets: the checked-in file references ${TRACKER_API_TOKEN}, and each engineer supplies their own value locally. Option B leaves a live credential in the repository and its history, which access controls do not cure. Option C abandons the shared config and distributes the secret over chat, trading one exposure for another. Option D relocates the hardcoded secret into committed source code — the same finding one directory over.

You built a personal scratchpad-notes MCP server and want it available in every Claude Code session on your laptop — client work, open source, everything — without touching any repository's shared configuration or re-adding it project by project.

Which configuration scope fits?

A. Project scope, adding it to each repository's .mcp.json file as you encounter them.
B. Local scope in each project, since the server itself runs locally over the stdio transport.
C. Project scope inside a template repository from which all of your future projects are forked.
D. User scope, which registers the server once for you and makes it available across all projects on the machine.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. User scope is the cross-project, personal option: configured once, available in every project you open, and invisible to teammates' shared configuration. Option A repeats setup per repository and pushes your personal tooling into files the whole team shares. Option B conflates the scope named local with the transport — local scope is still per-project, so the server would need re-adding everywhere. Option C only covers repositories descended from the template and still edits shared project configuration to solve a personal need.

column2:
A developer wires three MCP servers into Claude Code — internal docs, the ticket tracker, and a read-only database — then asks whether one conversation can pull a ticket, look up the customer in the database, and cite a runbook, or whether that takes three separate sessions.

What should you tell them?

A. One session per server: Claude Code binds each conversation to a single MCP connection at startup, chosen from the configured list.
B. One conversation works: the host holds a client connection to each server and offers the tools from all of them to the model together.
C. It can work in one session only if the three servers are first merged into a single server process that exposes all of the tools.
D. It works only if the user issues a command to switch the active server before each cross-server tool call, since one server is active at a time.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. The host creates one client per configured server and aggregates what they expose, so tools from all three servers sit in the model's tool list simultaneously and can be chained freely within one conversation. Option A invents a one-connection-per-conversation restriction that contradicts the one-client-per-server architecture. Option C demands a server merge that the architecture makes unnecessary. Option D imagines a manual server-switching mode; selection happens per tool call by the model, not through user routing commands.
